title: My days — and the little words that always take second place
goal: Describe your daily routine, use *se* for actions that turn back on yourself, and learn the placement rule that governs all of Bosnian's little words at once.
bekal: describing daily and weekly routines with *se* verbs
putting *sam, se, mi, ga, li* in second place, and knowing their order when they pile up
naming the days of the week and saying "every Monday"

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kako izgleda tvoj dan?
dialogs.intro: A long queue at the police counter. Amina turns to Budi, and her questions start with the simplest one.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Kako izgleda tvoj dan? Kada ustaješ?
lines.id: What's your day like? When do you get up?
lines.literal: how it-looks your-m day? when you-get-up?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ustajem u šest. Tuširam se, oblačim se i pijem kafu.
lines.id: I get up at six. I shower, get dressed and drink coffee.
lines.literal: I-get-up at six. I-shower self, I-dress self and I-drink coffee-acc.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: U šest? Ja se budim tek u sedam i po.
lines.id: At six? I don't wake up till half past seven.
lines.literal: at six? I self I-wake only-then at seven and half.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Navikao sam. U Jakarti sam ustajao u pet.
lines.id: I'm used to it. In Jakarta I got up at five.
lines.literal: used-m I-am. in Jakarta-loc I-am got-up-m at five.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: When do you get to work?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: U osam. Radim do pet, pa se vraćam kući.
lines.id: At eight. I work till five, then I go home.
lines.literal: at eight. I-work until five, then self I-return home.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: And what do you do in the evening?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ponedjeljkom, srijedom i petkom idem na kurs. Ostale dane se odmaram.
lines.id: Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays I go to class. The other days I rest.
lines.literal: Monday-ins, Wednesday-ins and Friday-ins I-go to course-acc. other-acc-pl day-pl self I-rest.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: A kad se odmaraš, šta radiš?
lines.id: And when you rest, what do you do?
lines.literal: and when self you-rest, what you-do?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Čitam, gledam filmove, ponekad se šetam pored rijeke.
lines.id: I read, watch films, sometimes walk along the river.
lines.literal: I-read, I-watch film-acc-pl, sometimes self I-walk beside river-gen.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Subotom spavam dugo. Nedjeljom se nalazim s Emirom.
lines.id: On Saturdays I sleep in. On Sundays I meet up with Emir.
lines.literal: Saturday-ins I-sleep long. Sunday-ins self I-meet with Emir-ins.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Znači, nikad ti nije dosadno. Dobro za tebe!
lines.id: So you're never bored. Good for you!
lines.literal: means, never to-you not-it-is boring. good for you-acc!

notes: **Notice that *se* moves around, yet always lands in the same spot according to its rule:** *Tuširam se* (after the first word), *Ja se budim* (after *ja*), *pa se vraćam* (after *pa*), *Ostale dane se odmaram*, *kad se odmaraš*. It never starts a sentence and is never far from second place. The full rule is below, and it applies to all the little words at once.

***Se* never changes.** One form for all six persons: *ja se tuširam, ti se tuširaš, on se tušira, mi se tuširamo*. That's a big relief compared with French or Spanish, which have six different forms.

***Ponedjeljkom, srijedom, petkom* mean "on Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays".** The form is the instrumental, the case that comes in Unit 16 — but this use stands on its own and is worth learning now, because it is the standard way to talk about weekly habits. Likewise *vikendom* (on weekends), *ljeti* (in summer), *jutrom* (in the mornings).

***Nikad ti nije dosadno* — a sentence with no subject.** Literally "never to you is it boring". Bosnian loves to build feelings this way: *hladno mi je* (I'm cold), *drago mi je* (I'm glad), *žao mi je* (I'm sorry), *dosadno mi je* (I'm bored). The person who feels is the receiver, not the subject. The pattern comes in Unit 13.

***Tek* means "only" in the sense of "not before": *tek u sedam* = not until seven.** Don't confuse it with *samo* (only, just) or *novo* (new). This little word is very common and learners often miss it.

grammars.title: Verbs with se
body: A large group of Bosnian verbs always travels with the little word *se*. Some you can guess, some you just have to learn — and some change meaning completely when the *se* is dropped.
after: ***Se* has three jobs.** First, **back to yourself**: *tuširam se* (I shower myself). Second, **each other**: *vidimo se* (we see each other = see you), *nalazimo se* (we meet), *poznajemo se* (we know each other). Third, **attached with no special meaning**: *bojim se, smijem se, nadam se* — this group can't be guessed and has to be learned together with the verb.

**Dropping *se* can change the meaning completely.** *Vraćam knjigu* = I'm returning the book; *vraćam se* = I'm going home. *Budim brata* = I wake my brother; *budim se* = I wake up. That's why this course always lists *se* as part of the verb, not as an extra.

***Se* also makes sentences with no subject** — Bosnian's way of saying "one" or "people" in general: *Kako se kaže…?* (how do you say…?), *Ovdje se ne puši* (no smoking here), *Kako se ide do centra?* (how do you get to the center?). It's a very useful pattern, and you'll see it on notice boards all the time.

**A small note that will matter in Unit 14:** in the past tense of *on/ona*, the word *je* is usually **dropped** when *se* is already there. *On se vratio* — not *on se je vratio*. In all other forms *se* and the helping verb live side by side: *ja sam se vratio, mi smo se vratili*.

grammars.title: Second place — one rule that governs everything
body: This is the most typical rule of the Slavic languages, and after this you have the whole toolkit. All the little words — *sam, si, je, se, mi, te, ga, li, ću* — compete for one spot: **right after the first word of the sentence**.

head: Order
The little words
Example
rows: *sam, si, smo, ste, su* · *ću, ćeš, će…*
dative: *mi, ti, mu, joj, nam, vam, im*
accusative: *me, te, ga, je, nas, vas, ih*

after: **The one rule: a little word may not start a sentence.** If there is no other word in front, the order flips: not *Se zovem Budi*, but *Zovem se Budi*. Not *Te čekam*, but *Čekam te* or *Ja te čekam*.
**The "first word" can be a whole phrase.** *Moja sestra se zove Sari* — *moja sestra* counts as one block, and the little word follows it. Likewise *Svaki dan se odmaram.*

**When several little words pile up, their order is exactly as in the table above** and never changes: *Jesi **li mu ga** dao?* (did you give it to him?) — *li*, then dative *mu*, then accusative *ga*. You don't need to build sentences that long yourself yet; what matters is knowing the order exists, so such sentences don't sound like random noise.

**Why does this matter at A1?** Because a word in the wrong place is far more noticeable than a wrong ending. A wrong ending makes you sound foreign; a little word at the start of a sentence makes you sound **broken** — native speakers pause for a moment to put it back. Practice three short sentences every day until the position feels natural: *Zovem se…* — *Drago mi je.* — *Vidimo se sutra.*

sections.title: Dani u sedmici — the days of the week

blocks.text: As in other Slavic languages, most Bosnian day names are not names but descriptions: *srijeda* means "middle", *četvrtak* "the fourth", *petak* "the fifth". The week starts on Monday, so the counting really does add up.

Three ways to place things on a day, all common: **u ponedjeljak** = on Monday (one particular day, accusative); **ponedjeljkom** = on Mondays (habit, instrumental); **svaki ponedjeljak** = every Monday, with a bit more emphasis. For today and the days around it: *danas* (today), *sutra* (tomorrow), *jučer* (yesterday), *prekosutra* (the day after tomorrow), *prekjučer* (the day before yesterday).

blocks.title: Friday in Bosnia
items: *Petak* is the day of Friday prayers (*džuma*) for Bosnian Muslims, and in Sarajevo around midday you'll see some offices slow down for a while. But **the official days off are still Saturday and Sunday**, as in the rest of Europe — so *vikend* means Saturday–Sunday, not Friday–Saturday.
What you'll hear as the weekend approaches: *Lijep vikend!* (have a nice weekend) and, on Friday afternoon, *Petak je!* — said in the same tone as anywhere else in the world.

blocks.text: Cover the Bosnian column, read the English, and rebuild the sentence from memory.

*Vidimo se sutra u deset i petnaest.*

items: On Mondays I go to class.
